title: What is the difference between static binding (compile-time — private/static/final methods, overloaded resolution on reference type) and dynamic binding (runtime — overridden instance methods, resolved on actual object type via vtable), and why does Parent p = new Child(); p.method() call Child's version?
shortTitle: What is static binding vs dynamic binding?

s1_definition.profdef: STATIC BINDING (early binding): the method call is resolved at COMPILE TIME. The compiler looks at the REFERENCE TYPE and binds directly. Used for: `private` methods (not inherited → no override possible), `static` methods (class-level → no vtable), `final` methods (sealed → no override), and overloaded methods (compiler picks signature by argument types). DYNAMIC BINDING (late binding): the method call is resolved at RUNTIME. The JVM looks at the ACTUAL OBJECT TYPE in the heap and dispatches via the virtual method table (vtable). Used for: overridden instance methods. `Parent p = new Child(); p.method()` calls Child's version because the JVM checks `p`'s actual type (Child) at runtime, not the variable type (Parent).
s1_definition.analogy: STATIC binding: the bank's directory says "for accounts, go to Counter 1." You look at the DIRECTORY (compile-time) and go there — doesn't matter WHO is sitting at Counter 1 today. DYNAMIC binding: you call customer service and say "I need help with my account." The system checks your ACTUAL account type (savings/current) at THAT MOMENT and routes you to the right specialist. The routing happens at the MOMENT of the call (runtime), not when the phone system was installed (compile-time).
s1_definition.oneliner: Static binding = compile-time, reference type, for private/static/final/overloaded. Dynamic binding = runtime, actual object type, for overridden instance methods (vtable dispatch). `Parent p = new Child(); p.method()` → dynamic → Child's version.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** STATIC BINDING (early binding): the method call is resolved at COMPILE TIME. The compiler looks at the REFERENCE TYPE and binds directly. Used for: `private` methods (not inherited → no override possible), `static` methods (class-level → no vtable), `final` methods (sealed → no override), and overloaded methods (compiler picks signature by argument types). DYNAMIC BINDING (late binding): the method call is resolved at RUNTIME. The JVM looks at the ACTUAL OBJECT TYPE in the heap and dispatches via the virtual method table (vtable). Used for: overridden instance methods. `Parent p = new Child(); p.method()` calls Child's version because the JVM checks `p`'s actual type (Child) at runtime, not the variable type (Parent).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** STATIC binding: the bank's directory says "for accounts, go to Counter 1." You look at the DIRECTORY (compile-time) and go there — doesn't matter WHO is sitting at Counter 1 today. DYNAMIC binding: you call customer service and say "I need help with my account." The system checks your ACTUAL account type (savings/current) at THAT MOMENT and routes you to the right specialist. The routing happens at the MOMENT of the call (runtime), not when the phone system was installed (compile-time).

**One line to remember:** Static binding = compile-time, reference type, for private/static/final/overloaded. Dynamic binding = runtime, actual object type, for overridden instance methods (vtable dispatch). `Parent p = new Child(); p.method()` → dynamic → Child's version.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — A developer assumed ALL methods dispatch dynamically.** Called `ref.getPolicy()` expecting SavingsAccount's policy — got Account's (static = compile-time binding). Called a private helper thinking it could be overridden — it can't (private = not inherited). The test proves: which methods use static binding and which use dynamic binding.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** `Account ref = new SavingsAccount()`. Variable type: Account. Actual object: SavingsAccount. Heap has SavingsAccount with its vtable.

**Step 2 — Dynamic.** `ref.getDescription()`. Compiler: "Account has getDescription? YES → valid." Bytecode: `invokevirtual Account.getDescription()`. Runtime: JVM checks actual type → SavingsAccount → vtable maps getDescription to SavingsAccount.getDescription → "Savings Account." RUNTIME decision.

**Step 3 — Static.** `ref.getPolicy()`. Compiler: "ref is Account. Account has static getPolicy()." Bytecode: `invokestatic Account.getPolicy()`. No runtime check. → "Standard." COMPILE-TIME decision.

**Step 4 — Summary.** Same reference (`ref`), same object. Instance method → dynamic (Child). Static method → static (Parent). This is WHY `Parent p = new Child(); p.method()` calls Child — instance methods use dynamic binding.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ STATIC BINDING (compile-time) ═══

  Method types: private, static, final, overloaded
  Resolution: COMPILER checks REFERENCE TYPE
  Bytecode: invokestatic / invokespecial (baked at compile time)
  No vtable lookup. Faster. No polymorphism.

  ═══ DYNAMIC BINDING (runtime) ═══

  Method types: overridden instance methods
  Resolution: JVM checks ACTUAL OBJECT TYPE at runtime
  Bytecode: invokevirtual → JVM does vtable lookup
  vtable: maps method → actual implementation

  ═══ EXAMPLE ═══

  Account ref = new SavingsAccount();

  ref.getDescription()  → DYNAMIC → SavingsAccount.getDescription() ← Child!
  ref.getPolicy()       → STATIC  → Account.getPolicy()             ← Parent!
  ref.getId()           → STATIC  → Account.getId()                  ← final!
  ref.callAudit()       → calls private audit() → STATIC → Account.audit()

  ═══ BINDING SUMMARY ═══

  private  → static binding (not inherited → no vtable entry)
  static   → static binding (class-level → no vtable)
  final    → static binding (sealed → JVM can inline)
  overload → static binding (compiler picks signature by args)
  override → DYNAMIC binding (JVM vtable dispatch at runtime) ← POLYMORPHISM!
```

```
  │ «abstract» Account                         │
  │ + calculateInterest()  (vtable slot 0)     │ ← DYNAMIC
  │ + static round(x)       (no vtable)        │ ← STATIC
  │ + final getId()         (no vtable)        │ ← STATIC

  Dispatch:
   REFERENCE TYPE  → static (compile-time, overload)
   ACTUAL OBJECT   → dynamic (runtime, override, vtable)

  JVM vtable: Account ref → heap obj header → klass ptr
              → method table → SavingsAccount.calcInterest
  SOLID: LSP (subtype substitutable via dynamic dispatch)
  Call chain: ref.calculateInterest() → vtable lookup →
              SavingsAccount.calculateInterest()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Static binding resolves method calls at compile time — the compiler looks at the REFERENCE TYPE and binds directly. Used for private methods (not inherited, no vtable entry), static methods (class-level, no vtable), final methods (sealed, JVM can inline), and overloaded methods (compiler picks signature by argument types). Dynamic binding resolves at runtime — the JVM looks at the ACTUAL OBJECT TYPE in the heap and dispatches via the vtable. Used for overridden instance methods — this IS runtime polymorphism.

`Parent p = new Child(); p.method()` calls Child's version because: the compiler generates `invokevirtual Parent.method()` (valid — Parent has the method). At runtime, the JVM checks `p`'s actual object → Child → looks up Child's vtable → finds Child.method() → calls it. The variable type (Parent) determined compile-time VALIDITY. The actual type (Child) determined runtime DISPATCH. This is why polymorphism works — and why static methods DON'T exhibit polymorphism (they use `invokestatic` which binds to the class at compile time, ignoring the actual object).

In my binding demo, the same reference `Account ref = new SavingsAccount()` produces different binding: `ref.getDescription()` → dynamic → "Savings Account" (Child). `ref.getPolicy()` → static → "Standard" (Parent). `ref.getId()` → static → "ACC-BASE" (final). Five method types, two binding mechanisms. The key insight for interviews: ALL instance method calls go through dynamic binding (invokevirtual) EXCEPT private, which uses invokespecial. Static uses invokestatic. Final uses invokevirtual but the JVM can optimize since no override exists.

keyPoints: Static binding: resolved at compile time — private, static, final methods + overloading
Dynamic binding: resolved at runtime — overridden instance methods
JVM uses vtable (virtual method table) for dynamic dispatch
Static binding is faster, dynamic binding enables polymorphism
